task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper explainer for general readers answering the question: Why do electric vehicle batteries catch fire, and how dangerous are those fires compared to conventional car fires? Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of February 7, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: Electric vehicle batteries use lithium-ion chemistry; energy is stored in the electrochemical reaction between a lithium-containing cathode, an anode typically made of graphite, and a liquid electrolyte.
Thermal runaway is a chain reaction in which one overheated cell transfers heat to neighboring cells, each of which releases more heat, until the battery pack catches fire or ruptures.
Triggers for thermal runaway include physical damage (collision or puncture), overcharging beyond design limits, manufacturing defects, and exposure to extreme heat.
Lithium-ion battery fires burn at temperatures that can exceed 1,000 degrees Celsius and produce toxic gases including hydrogen fluoride, which is extremely hazardous.
EV battery fires reignite repeatedly as neighboring cells reach their thermal threshold; firefighters often need to cool the battery continuously for hours to prevent reignition.

Vehicle safety engineer Dr. Tomás Lindgren of Northview Automotive Institute said: "The fire itself is not necessarily more likely in an EV. The challenge is the duration and the chemical toxicity of the gases, which are different from a gasoline fire."

U.S. fire safety data from the National Automotive Safety Institute shows EVs have a lower fire rate per vehicle-mile traveled than gasoline vehicles, but EV fires take longer to extinguish when they do occur.

Battery management systems monitor cell voltage, temperature, and current to prevent overcharge and overtemperature; a failure or bypass of these systems is the most common pathway to thermal runaway.

High-speed DC fast charging produces more heat in cells than slower AC charging and is more likely to trigger thermal runaway if a cell has a manufacturing defect; most EV manufacturers recommend limiting fast charging frequency.

Solid-state batteries, which replace liquid electrolyte with a solid material, are considered inherently safer because they do not contain the flammable liquid electrolyte; they are not yet in commercial mass production.

Garage fires involving EVs have raised concerns because the fires can spread to the building structure before responders arrive; some fire safety officials recommend not parking EVs in enclosed garages if the battery is damaged.
Fire departments in major cities have developed EV-specific protocols, including the use of large volumes of water applied continuously; some departments use immersion containers for small vehicles.

Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery chemistry is considered more thermally stable than nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) chemistry; some manufacturers have shifted toward LFP for standard-range vehicles.

Dr. Lindgren said the industry's response to thermal runaway risk has focused on cell-level isolation — design features that prevent one failing cell from triggering its neighbor — rather than eliminating the root cause.
Regulatory testing for EV batteries includes nail penetration tests, overcharge tests, and thermal propagation tests, all designed to simulate abuse conditions.
EV manufacturers are required to disclose battery safety data including the results of abuse testing; access to that data for third-party researchers varies by company.

Hydrogen fuel cell vehicles do not use lithium-ion batteries for primary propulsion and do not carry the same thermal runaway risk, though compressed hydrogen storage has its own safety considerations.

Dr. Lindgren said the public perception of EV fire risk is disproportionate to the statistical rate: gasoline vehicle fires number in the hundreds of thousands per year in the U.S.; EV fires are in the thousands.
The National Automotive Safety Institute said it is working with federal regulators to develop standardized post-crash battery inspection protocols for first responders.
Battery manufacturers are researching fire-retardant electrolyte additives and ceramic separators to slow thermal propagation even if a cell fails.

forbidden_additions: a claim that EV fires are more common per mile than gasoline vehicle fires
a fire temperature different from 1,000 degrees Celsius
a claim that solid-state batteries are commercially available
